title: The Accidental Quadratic
subtitle: Small n is fine. Then the data grows.
options: const seen = new Set(); for (const id of ids) { if (seen.has(id)) continue; seen.add(id); process(id); }
for (const a of items) { if (others.includes(a.id)) { flagged.push(a); } }
hints: Which operation is O(m) per call on arrays but O(1) on Sets?

solution.summary: The correct answer is C — for (const a of items) { if (others.includes(a.id)) { flagged.push(a); } }
solution.answer: for (const a of items) { if (others.includes(a.id)) { flagged.push(a); } }
reasoning: Nested full scans hide behind clean loop syntax; the array-method version reads like it is "just a filter".
The universal fix: hoist the lookup into a hash-based structure once, then query it per iteration.
whyNot: const seen = new Set(); for (const id of ids) { if (seen.has(id)) continue; seen.add(id); process(id); } — This one is linear thanks to the Set — constant-time membership checks.
items.forEach((x) => totals.push(x.price * x.qty)) — Pushing to an array per element is amortized O(1) — linear overall.
const merged = [...first, ...second] — A single spread is O(n+m) once.
